title: Cervical Cancer Cases in India Drop 37% Over a Decade, Driven by Screening and Vaccination Push
excerpt: Data from India's cancer registries shows a significant decline in cervical cancer incidence rates over the past decade, as opportunistic screening expands and the country rolls out its first nationwide HPV vaccination campaign.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Cervical cancer incidence in India has decreased by 37% over the last decade.
  • Jharkhand and Himachal Pradesh saw the largest declines in cervical cancer rates, over 50% and 48.3%, respectively.
  • India's first nationwide HPV vaccination campaign targets 11.5 million girls aged 14, launched in February 2026.
  • Despite progress, India accounts for 20% of global cervical cancer cases and 25% of deaths annually.
  • Age-standardized cervical cancer incidence rates in India have fallen by approximately 37% over the past decade, according to data from the National Cancer Registry Programme and the Global Burden of Disease study.
  • The decline is attributed to improved personal hygiene, increased opportunistic screening, rising age at marriage, and expanded awareness — though organized screening still covers fewer than 2% of Indian women.
  • India launched its first nationwide HPV vaccination campaign in February 2026, targeting 11.5 million girls aged 14 with free Gardasil doses at government health facilities.
  • Despite the progress, India still accounts for roughly one-fifth of all global cervical cancer cases and one-quarter of deaths, with an estimated 127,000 new diagnoses and 80,000 fatalities annually.

A Measurable Decline in a Persistent Killer

Cervical cancer incidence rates in India have dropped by approximately 37% over the past decade, a decline that health officials and researchers attribute to a combination of opportunistic screening, shifting social indicators, and early vaccination pilots in select states. The data, drawn from India's National Cancer Registry Programme (NCRP) and corroborated by the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2019 study, marks a significant turn in the country's long battle against one of its deadliest cancers, according to reports in The Indian Express and Health and Me.

The trend is not uniform across states. According to the GBD study published in BMC Cancer, Jharkhand recorded the steepest decline in cervical cancer incidence — over 50% — from 1990 to 2019, followed by Himachal Pradesh at 48.3%. Tamil Nadu, while showing improvement, continues to report the highest absolute incidence in the country, while Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh register the lowest.

The age-standardized incidence rate for India showed a statistically significant decline, with an average annual percentage change (AAPC) of −0.82% from 1990 to 2019, and the sharpest dip occurring between 1998 and 2005, when the AAPC reached −3.22%, according to the same study.

What's Behind the Numbers

Researchers point to several socioeconomic and behavioral shifts driving the decline. Improved personal hygiene, cleaner living conditions, increasing use of opportunistic screening programs, and delayed age at marriage and first pregnancy have all contributed, according to the South Asian Journal of Cancer. These factors reduce exposure to the human papillomavirus (HPV), which causes nearly all cervical cancers.

In rural West Bengal, a pooled analysis of three screening studies spanning 2001 to 2021 found that detection rates of high-grade cervical precancer (CIN 2+) dropped from 5.7 per 1,000 women to 2 per 1,000 — a 65% decline. Higher education and delayed marriage were independently associated with lower risk, according to the study published in Cancer Epidemiology.

"According to the GBD study published in BMC Cancer, Jharkhand recorded the steepest decline in cervical cancer incidence — over 50% — from 1990 to 2019, followed by Himachal Pradesh at 48.3%."

"The observed decline in CIN 2+ prevalence can be attributed to improved education, delayed age at marriage, reduced fertility rate and women's empowerment."

— Cancer Epidemiology study on cervical precancer trends in West Bengal, 2025

Vaccination has also played a limited but growing role. Sikkim and Punjab introduced HPV vaccines through state-level immunization programs as early as 2016. But nationally, fewer than 1% of Indian women had received an HPV vaccine before the 2026 campaign launch, according to a review published in the journal Cancer.

The 2026 Vaccination Campaign Changes the Calculus

On February 28, 2026, Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched India's first nationwide HPV vaccination campaign in Ajmer, Rajasthan. The campaign makes the quadrivalent Gardasil vaccine available free at government health facilities — primary health centres, community health centres, district hospitals, and government medical colleges — for approximately 11.5 million girls aged 14 across the country.

The rollout is supported by Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, which has supplied doses as part of a global effort to reach the World Health Organization's 90-70-90 elimination targets for 2030: 90% of girls vaccinated by age 15, 70% of women screened by ages 35 and 45, and 90% of those diagnosed receiving treatment.

"India's introduction of the HPV vaccine and its plan to vaccinate more than 10 million girls each year will have a profound impact not only nationally but also globally."

— Partha Basu, Head of Early Detection, Prevention & Infections Branch, International Agency for Research on Cancer

India's Serum Institute has also developed an indigenous quadrivalent vaccine, Cervavac, which was introduced in 2023 and is available privately for ₹1,200–1,700 per dose. The Indian Council of Medical Research launched a single-dose study for Cervavac in November 2024 among girls aged 9–14, results of which could simplify future roll-outs.

Screening Remains the Weak Link

Despite the incidence decline, India's formal screening infrastructure lags far behind its ambition. As of February 2026, 8.73 crore (87.3 million) women had been screened for cervical cancer, according to the National NCD Portal — a fraction of the estimated 453 million women aged 15 and above at risk.

Fewer than 2% of Indian women undergo cervical cancer screening, and the country still lacks an organized, population-based screening program. Officials at a recent government summit flagged HPV DNA-based testing, including self-sampling, as a "game-changer" for reaching women in rural and underserved areas, where the disease burden is heaviest.

Aradhana Patnaik, Additional Secretary of the National Health Mission, called cervical cancer elimination "an achievable goal for India," while emphasizing the need for rapid expansion of both vaccination access and screening infrastructure, particularly high-performance HPV DNA tests.

What This Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, the progress carries both reassurance and urgency. Relatives in India — particularly in rural areas and states with high incidence like Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, and Uttar Pradesh — may still face limited access to screening and vaccination. Diaspora families can play a role by raising awareness about the HPV vaccine's availability and safety, helping counter persistent myths and hesitancy that health officials say remain a vulnerability for the national campaign.

In the private healthcare sector, where many diaspora-connected families seek care, the availability of Cervavac alongside Gardasil gives additional options for those willing to pay out-of-pocket for earlier or broader coverage beyond the government programme's age criteria.

The Road Ahead

The 37% decline marks genuine progress, but the absolute numbers remain staggering. India still records roughly 127,000 new cervical cancer cases and 80,000 deaths each year, according to WHO estimates for 2022. The National Centre for Disease Informatics and Research projects approximately 79,239 new cases and 42,789 cervical cancer deaths in 2025 alone.

Impact of HPV Vaccination Campaign
›11.5 million girls targeted for vaccination
›Free Gardasil doses available at government facilities
›Supported by Gavi, aiming for WHO's 90-70-90 targets
›Cervavac introduced in 2023, priced ₹1,200–1,700 per dose

Experts estimate that if India achieves 80–100% vaccination coverage alongside two lifetime screenings per woman, cervical cancer could be eliminated as a public health problem by 2070–79, according to a Lancet study cited by Prashant Mathur, director of the National Centre for Disease Informatics and Research in Bengaluru.

The vaccination campaign will resume in 2027 to cover the next cohort of eligible girls. Whether India can sustain coverage, scale up screening, and overcome hesitancy will determine if the current decade's gains accelerate into something transformative — or stall at a statistical footnote.
